Only the monthly plan. Digital content and features consumed inside the app must go through StoreKit or Play Billing; physical goods and real-world services are forbidden from using it and go through your own payment processor.

### What the store keeps for itself
- Subscriptions, permanent unlocks, level packs, in-game currency, removing ads — anything that only exists inside your app. Apple's guideline 3.1.1 and Google Play's Payments policy both say so.
- With that comes the store's price tiers and currencies, the store's refund decisions, and a commission of 30%, or 15% under Apple's Small Business Program and Play's reduced rate on the first $1M a year.

### What must not use it
- Physical goods, shipping, event tickets, rides, food delivery, and services a human performs in the real world. Apple 3.1.5 rejects apps that put those through IAP.
- Charitable donations to a registered nonprofit. On iOS a tip to a creator for digital content does go through IAP; a one-off gift where 100% reaches the recipient does not.

### The exceptions in 2026
- US storefront: after the 2025 rulings in Epic v. Apple and Epic v. Google an app may point users at a web checkout. Apple's contempt order stripped both the commission and the warning sheet from those links; Google's injunction bars it from requiring Play Billing or blocking the link. Neither is the default outside the US.
- EU: the DMA opens alternative payment options and external offers, on Apple's own fee terms.
- Reader apps and multiplatform services can link to an external account page, provided the catalogue is not also sold in-app.

Rule of thumb: if the thing bought is only real inside your app, the store bills it; if it exists in the world, the store must not. The exceptions are jurisdiction-shaped and move every year, so keep the mapping in server config rather than in a developer's memory.

The coins must be consumed after your server credits them, the unlock must never be persisted locally because the store remembers it forever, and the subscription has a lifecycle the client never sees, so it can only ever read the current state from your backend.

### Consumable — the 500 coins
- Play: call `consumeAsync` only after your server has credited the balance. Consuming makes the token vanish; consume first and crash, and the coins are gone with no way to replay them. Not consuming at all means the user cannot buy that pack again.
- StoreKit: `.consumable` transactions never appear in `Transaction.currentEntitlements`, so `finish()` is the same one-way door. The balance lives on your server — a local counter is unrecoverable on reinstall.

### Non-consumable — the ad-free unlock
- The store owns this fact permanently. iOS returns it from `Transaction.currentEntitlements` for that Apple Account; Play returns it from `queryPurchasesAsync(INAPP)` for as long as you never consumed it.
- The client stores nothing. It asks — which is what makes restore on a new device a query rather than a recovery.

### Auto-renewing — the monthly plan
- Renewals, cancellations, billing failures and refunds all happen on the store's servers while your app is not running, so the expiry date you cached last launch is already suspect.
- Play models one subscription product with base plans and offers; the client must pass the chosen offer's `offerToken` into the billing flow. StoreKit exposes `Product.SubscriptionInfo.Status` with a `RenewalState` — subscribed, expired, inBillingRetryPeriod, inGracePeriod, revoked.

The fourth type, non-renewing (`.nonRenewable` on iOS, modelled as a one-time product on Play), is the one where the store tracks nothing: you store the end date and you stack renewals yourself.

Rule of thumb: the client persists nothing the store or your server can be asked for. The only durable state it owns is "which purchase have I not yet reported".

Every purchase that does not come back through that call site: pending approvals, purchases completed while the app was dead, renewals, buys made on another device, and App Store promoted purchases that never touched your paywall.

### The flow
1. Load products from the store — `Product.products(for:)`, or `queryProductDetailsAsync` on Play. Never render a price you hardcoded.
2. Start the flow, tagging it with your user id: `.appAccountToken(uuid)` on StoreKit, `setObfuscatedAccountId` on Play.
3. The store hands back a `VerificationResult<Transaction>`, or a `Purchase` carrying a purchase token.
4. Send that identifier to your backend, which asks the store's server API whether it is real and current, and writes the entitlement.
5. Refresh entitlement from your backend. This is where the feature turns on.
6. Only now `finish()` the transaction, or acknowledge it on Play.

### The purchases that call site never sees
- **Pending**: Ask to Buy and slow payment methods return `.pending` on StoreKit and `PurchaseState.PENDING` on Play, and the real transaction arrives hours later. No money has moved yet, so nothing may be granted.
- The process was killed between the payment sheet and your continuation.
- Renewals, and anything bought on a second device signed into the same store account.
- A promoted in-app purchase started from the App Store product page, which launches your app straight into a transaction.

So the actual entry point is an always-on listener started before any UI: `Transaction.updates` on iOS, `PurchasesUpdatedListener` plus a `queryPurchasesAsync` sweep on every resume and reconnect on Android. Also drain `Transaction.unfinished` at launch.

Mental model: the paywall's job is to *start* a purchase; the listener's job is to *complete* one. Handle only the callback and you ship an app that is perfect in the sandbox and loses real money in production.

Acknowledgement. Google Play automatically refunds and revokes any purchase that is not acknowledged or consumed within three days, and the users find out before you do.

### Google
- A one-time product is settled with `consumeAsync` for a consumable (which also acknowledges it) or `acknowledgePurchase` for a non-consumable. A subscription is acknowledged on the initial purchase and on any replacement — upgrade, downgrade, resubscribe. Plain renewals need nothing.
- The clock starts when the purchase reaches `PurchaseState.PURCHASED`, not when it was created, so a PENDING purchase must be left alone until it converts.
- Prefer acknowledging from your server via `purchases.subscriptions.acknowledge` / `purchases.products.acknowledge`, right after the entitlement row is written. The client acknowledging first means a crash on the way to your backend leaves an acknowledged purchase with no grant behind it.

### Apple
- `transaction.finish()` is not the same promise. Nothing is refunded if you skip it — but the transaction is redelivered through `Transaction.updates` on every launch and stays in `Transaction.unfinished` forever, so a "purchase that keeps popping up" is almost always a missing `finish()`.
- That makes `finish()` a bad unlock signal in either direction: it tells StoreKit you have delivered, and it tells your UI nothing.

### The ordering that survives a crash
1. Verify the identifier server-side.
2. Write the entitlement or credit the balance, durably.
3. Acknowledge, or `finish()`.
4. Refresh the UI from the entitlement.

Doing 3 before 2 is the trade you never want: for a non-consumable the purchase is still queryable so you recover, but for a consumable, `consumeAsync` before the credit lands destroys the only record that the user paid.

Rule of thumb: acknowledging means "I have delivered the goods." Say it only when you have.

A boolean cannot express the four things entitlement actually is — who owns it, until when, from which platform and in what state — so it goes wrong for paying customers long before anybody tries to cheat it.

### What honest users hit
- New phone, or a reinstall: the flag is gone and a paid-up subscriber is looking at your paywall.
- Cancelled in the store, expired, or a card that failed: the store never calls your app, so the flag stays true and a lapsed user keeps premium indefinitely.
- Refunded: exactly the same, in the direction that costs you money.
- Subscribed on iOS, opened the Android app or the web app: each install owns its own boolean, so the three disagree.
- In grace period the truth is "paid, but the card failed". A boolean can only say yes or no, so the UI cannot ask them to fix it and the subscription dies silently.

### What the client reads instead
- One entitlement record from your backend: `productId`, `status` — active, grace, on hold, expired — `expiresAt`, `willRenew`, and `source` so you can tell an App Store subscription from a Play one or from a promo grant.
- Cached with the time it was fetched, and refreshed on launch, on foreground, after any purchase, and when a silent push says server state changed.
- An offline policy chosen deliberately: honour a cached *active* entitlement for a bounded window — renewals are monthly, a day of slack costs nothing — and never grant a *new* entitlement while offline.

Rule of thumb: the client caches an answer, the server owns the question. If your app can be confidently right about entitlement without ever talking to your backend, the model is wrong.

The server exchanges the identifier for the store's current view of that purchase, because a signature only proves the payload came from the store when it was issued — not that it is still valid, and not that it belongs to this user.

### Apple
- The client sends `transaction.originalID`, or the signed JWS itself. The server calls the App Store Server API — `GET /inApps/v1/subscriptions/{originalTransactionId}` for status, `/inApps/v2/history/{originalTransactionId}` for history — authenticating with an ES256 JWT signed by an in-app purchase key from App Store Connect.
- Responses are signed JWS too. Verify the `x5c` chain up to Apple's root before trusting a single field. Apple ships the App Store Server Library for Java, Python, Node and Swift that does the chain verification and decoding; hand-rolling it is how teams end up trusting an unverified header.
- The old `/verifyReceipt` endpoint is deprecated — new work uses the Server API.

### Google
- The client sends the `purchaseToken` and product id. The server calls `purchases.subscriptionsv2.get` or `purchases.products.get` on the Play Developer API with a service account, and reads `subscriptionState`, `lineItems[].expiryTime` and `linkedPurchaseToken`.
- The trap is `linkedPurchaseToken`: on an upgrade, downgrade or resubscribe Play issues a *new* token and points it at the old one. A server that stores tokens without following that link grows two live subscriptions for one paying user.

### Why on-device verification is not validation
- The clock, the SDK and the process all belong to the user, and a signature check running inside the app can be patched out of it.
- Even a genuinely verified signature is a snapshot. It cannot know about the refund, cancellation or chargeback that happened after it was signed.
- A payload that verifies is also replayable: one leaked transaction, posted to your claim endpoint from a hundred devices, is a hundred grants unless the store id is stored under a unique constraint.

Mental model: the identifier is a claim check, not a ticket. Your server redeems it with the store and then trusts only its own record.

Both stores push lifecycle events to an endpoint you register — App Store Server Notifications V2 and Play's Real-time Developer Notifications over Pub/Sub — and the only handler that stays correct treats a notification as a hint to re-fetch state, never as the state itself.

### Apple
- One HTTPS URL per environment, set in App Store Connect. The body is a signed JWS: verify it to Apple's root before reading a field.
- The types that move entitlement: `SUBSCRIBED`, `DID_RENEW`, `DID_FAIL_TO_RENEW` with subtype `GRACE_PERIOD`, `EXPIRED`, `DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_STATUS`, `REFUND`, `REVOKE`.
- Return 200 fast and do the work after. Apple retries a failed delivery on a backoff over about three days, and `GET /inApps/v1/notifications/history` lets you backfill what you still lost.

### Google
- RTDN publishes to a Pub/Sub topic you own; your service subscribes to it. The message carries a purchase token and a notification type, deliberately not the subscription state — Google's own guidance is to call `purchases.subscriptionsv2.get` and treat that as truth. Refunds and chargebacks arrive as `voidedPurchaseNotification`.
- Pub/Sub is at-least-once and unordered, so duplicates and out-of-order arrivals are normal traffic. Ack every message you parsed, including types you do not handle, or the backlog grows forever.

### Making the handler idempotent
- Dedupe on the store's own id — Apple's `notificationUUID`, Pub/Sub's `messageId` — inserted into a processed table with a unique constraint, so a redelivery becomes a no-op.
- Never apply a delta. Write the absolute state you just fetched, guarded by a monotonic field — Apple's `signedDate`, Play's expiry time — so an older event arriving late cannot overwrite a newer one.
- Commit the entitlement row and the processed-id row in one transaction, so a retry either redoes it cleanly or skips it.
- Keep a reconciliation job over subscriptions expiring soon. A dropped notification is either free premium or a wrongly locked-out customer.

Mental model: a notification says only "something changed for this token". What it changed *to* is a question you ask the store's API.

At which store account is signed in on the device, and at what kind of product they bought — restore reads what the *store account* owns, not what your app account paid for.

### What restore actually is
- iOS: the entitlement is already available. `Transaction.currentEntitlements` yields every non-consumable and active auto-renewable for the Apple Account signed into the App Store, with no prompt and no user action. `AppStore.sync()` is the heavy hammer behind the Restore button — it re-authenticates, so call it only from an explicit tap. Apple requires that button in any app selling non-consumables or non-renewing subscriptions.
- Android: there is no restore API. `queryPurchasesAsync` returns the active, unconsumed purchases for the Google account on the device, and "Restore" is that query plus a re-sync with your backend.

### What it cannot bring back
- Consumables. Coins you already consumed are gone from the store's view; only your server's balance remembers them, which is the whole argument for keeping the balance there.
- Anything bought under a different store account. A second Apple Account or Google account restores nothing, and no code of yours can fix that — the user has to sign back in.
- An expired subscription. Restore returns entitlement, not money.
- A purchase from the other platform. An iOS subscription does not restore on Android; that needs an account link, not a restore.

### What the app does with the result
- Send whatever came back to your backend and let it reconcile, because a restore is a claim: the server still decides whether that transaction is already bound to somebody else's account.
- Always show an explicit outcome, including "nothing to restore on this account", and say which store account was checked. A silent no-op is the single largest source of restore support tickets.

Rule of thumb: Restore is a re-sync from store account to your account, not a recovery tool.

The store account owns the payment and your account owns the entitlement, so the link between the two is something you create at purchase time and enforce on your server — neither store enforces it for you.

### Bind at purchase
- iOS: pass `.appAccountToken(uuid)` to `product.purchase(options:)`. It must be a UUID, so map your user id to one; it comes back on the transaction and inside App Store Server Notifications.
- Android: `setObfuscatedAccountId()` on `BillingFlowParams` (plus `setObfuscatedProfileId()` if one account has several profiles). It surfaces on `purchases.subscriptionsv2.get` under `externalAccountIdentifiers`.
- Both are hints, not locks. A restore on a device signed into a different app account arrives with no token at all, and the store will not stop it.

### Enforce on the server
- Put a unique constraint on the store identifier — Apple's `originalTransactionId`, Play's purchase token — pointing at exactly one user id. The first account to claim it owns it.
- A second account presenting the same identifier gets a conflict, not a quiet second entitlement. Show "this subscription is already active on another account" with a way back into that account; transfers are a logged support action.

### Two traps
- **Family Sharing** gives the same subscription to up to five more Apple IDs. Those transactions have `ownershipType == .familyShared` and none of your `appAccountToken`, so an ownership rule written for the buyer alone rejects five legitimate people.
- **`linkedPurchaseToken`**: when a Play user resubscribes or upgrades, the new purchase carries a pointer to the token it replaced. Fail to retire the old row and you keep granting access on a token that will never renew again.

The store tells you a payment happened. Only your database can say whose it is.

The store decides introductory-offer eligibility and enforces it at purchase, so a paywall promising a trial the store will not grant is a UI bug: you have to ask before you render.

### Apple's four offer types
- **Introductory offer** — one per subscription group per Apple ID, ever. Ask `product.subscription?.isEligibleForIntroOffer` and render the regular price when it comes back false.
- **Promotional offer** — for current or lapsed subscribers, and here *you* pick who qualifies. It only works with a `Product.SubscriptionOffer.Signature` your server produces with the in-app purchase key; the app must never hold that key.
- **Offer code** — redeemed in the App Store or in-app through `AppStore.presentOfferCodeRedeemSheet(in:)`.
- **Win-back offer** (iOS 18+) — configured in App Store Connect for lapsed subscribers, surfaced by the App Store itself and readable in-app as `product.subscription?.winBackOffers`.

### Play's model
- The base plan holds the price; offers hang off it with `offerTags`, `pricingPhases` and an `offerToken`, and eligibility is a condition you set in Play Console (new customer, developer-determined, or an upgrade).
- The trap is the token: `launchBillingFlow` charges whatever `offerToken` you passed. Send the base plan's token while the paywall says "7 days free" and the user is billed immediately.

### The rule
Eligibility belongs to the *store* account, not yours — someone with a second Apple ID can genuinely take the trial twice, and any abuse limit you care about has to live on your server, keyed by your user id.

Between "renewed" and "gone" both stores run a recovery window — billing retry, an optional grace period, and on Play an account hold — and access continues only during the grace part.

### Apple
- `Product.SubscriptionInfo.RenewalState` is the client view: `.subscribed`, `.inGracePeriod`, `.inBillingRetryPeriod`, `.expired`, `.revoked`.
- Billing grace period is opt-in in App Store Connect. While it runs the transaction stays in `currentEntitlements`, so access continues; without it, a failed renewal expires immediately.
- Server-side you see `DID_FAIL_TO_RENEW` (subtype `GRACE_PERIOD`), then `GRACE_PERIOD_EXPIRED`, then `EXPIRED` with subtype `BILLING_RETRY` if it never recovered.

### Google
- `purchases.subscriptionsv2.get` returns `subscriptionState`: `ACTIVE`, `IN_GRACE_PERIOD`, `ON_HOLD`, `PAUSED`, `CANCELED`, `EXPIRED`, `PENDING`.
- Grace period is configured in Play Console (up to 30 days, access continues); account hold follows for up to 30 more days with access revoked while Play keeps retrying; `PAUSED` is a pause the user chose.
- RTDN carries each transition: `SUBSCRIPTION_IN_GRACE_PERIOD`, `SUBSCRIPTION_ON_HOLD`, `SUBSCRIPTION_RECOVERED`, `SUBSCRIPTION_RESTARTED`.

### What the UI does
- Grace or retry: keep access, show a dismissible banner that deep-links to the fix — `BillingClient.showInAppMessages` on Android, the `Message.Reason.billingIssue` sheet or `AppStore.showManageSubscriptions(in:)` on iOS.
- Hold or expired: revoke, and offer resubscribe without losing their data.
- **`CANCELED` is not `EXPIRED`.** A cancelled subscriber keeps full access until the expiry date; showing them a paywall the moment they cancel is the most common bug here.

Model the subscription as a state machine, never as a boolean.

You change the price in App Store Connect or Play Console and the store handles notice, currency, tax and billing; the only piece you own is the consent case, where the subscription simply stops renewing if the user never agrees.

### Apple
- Prices are per-storefront price points. An increase for existing subscribers renews automatically after notice if it happens at most once a year and stays within Apple's limits — 50% and $5 for periods under a year, 50% and $50 for annual. Anything larger needs explicit consent.
- Consent arrives as a StoreKit message: iterate `Message.messages` and call `message.display(in: scene)`. Defer it while a purchase or a video is on screen, but never drop it — an unshown sheet is a subscriber who silently lapses.
- `renewalInfo.priceIncreaseStatus` reports `.pending` or `.agreed`; the server sees `PRICE_INCREASE` with subtype `PENDING` then `ACCEPTED`.

### Google
- Prices are per-region on the base plan, and you choose in Play Console whether existing subscribers migrate or stay in a legacy price cohort. Play runs the notification and the consent itself, then sends `SUBSCRIPTION_PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED`.
- Do not build a screen for it: `launchPriceChangeConfirmationFlow` was deprecated in Billing Library 5 and removed in 6.

### What is still yours
- Never render a hard-coded or server-configured price. `product.displayPrice` and `pricingPhases.formattedPrice` are already localized for that user's storefront, and anything else eventually disagrees with the charge.
- Update store metadata, screenshots and paywall copy in the same release — a screenshot showing the old price outlives your changelog.

In your own database, keyed by your own user id: a store transaction is evidence, and the entitlement row it produces is the single thing every client reads.

### The shape
- One entitlement row per user and product — `state`, `active_until`, `source` (`APP_STORE` / `PLAY` / `STRIPE`), `source_ref` — written only by your server.
- Store credentials live in a separate table with a unique key per `originalTransactionId`, purchase token or Stripe subscription id, each pointing at a user. A user can accumulate several; the entitlement is their union.
- Renewals arrive from three directions — App Store Server Notifications v2, Play RTDN, Stripe webhooks — and all three converge on the same row. Every handler is idempotent because all three retry.
- Clients read `GET /entitlements`. StoreKit's `currentEntitlements` and Play's `queryPurchasesAsync` are the offline fallback and the reconciliation input, never the answer.

### What goes wrong
- **Double billing.** An iOS subscriber opens Android, the paywall does not know, and they pay twice. Resolve entitlement before rendering a paywall, and when it is active elsewhere show a management hint instead of a buy button — you cannot cancel an Apple subscription from Android.
- Cancellation belongs where the purchase happened: `AppStore.showManageSubscriptions(in:)`, Play's subscription URL, or your web billing portal.
- Trust the store's expiry timestamps, never the device clock, and cache the verdict with a short TTL so a flight does not lock a paying user out.

Stores are payment processors. The subscription is your data — treat any client-side entitlement check as a cache of a server fact.

Three layers, each catching a different class of bug: an Xcode StoreKit configuration file for everything local, the store sandboxes for the real client-to-store round trip, and test notifications for your webhook.

### Local, no store at all
- A `.storekit` file defines products, prices, offers and subscription groups, and Xcode's Transaction Manager forces refunds, Ask to Buy, billing retry and price increases on demand. Renewals are compressed — a month can pass in a minute.
- `SKTestSession` does the same from tests: `buyProduct`, `expireSubscription`, `forceRenewalOfSubscription`, `refundTransaction`, `setSimulatedError`. That turns "what happens on refund" into a CI assertion instead of a manual ritual.

### Sandbox and license testers
- Apple: a Sandbox Apple Account, accelerated renewals (a month runs in five minutes) capped at a dozen renewals, and a per-tester renewal rate you can set in App Store Connect. TestFlight builds use the sandbox too.
- Play: license testers listed in Play Console, the build installed from an internal or closed track with the real signing and version code, and test cards that always decline — the only way to reach account hold.
- Your backend: the App Store Server API's request-a-test-notification endpoint and a hand-published Pub/Sub message prove the webhook is reachable, verified and idempotent.

### What none of it reproduces
- Real money: chargebacks, tax, refund decisions, and the real multi-week billing-retry timing.
- Real storefront pricing, Family Sharing across real Apple IDs, and store review running its own purchase.
- Environment mismatch. Branch on `transaction.environment` (or the notification's environment field), not on a build flag, or a sandbox tester's data lands in production tables.

Start from the identifier on the receipt — both stores let your server turn an order id into the real transaction, so the fix is a server-side lookup and a grant, never "please buy it again".

### From a receipt to a transaction
- Apple: the emailed receipt carries an **order ID**, not a transaction id. `GET /inApps/v1/lookup/{orderId}` on the App Store Server API returns the signed transactions behind it, and `/inApps/v1/transactions/{transactionId}` plus the v2 history endpoint take it from there — all with the same signed JWT your validation already uses.
- Google: the receipt shows a `GPA.…` order id. Play Console's order management maps it to the purchase token, and `purchases.subscriptionsv2.get` or `purchases.products.get` gives you the state.
- Check which store account paid before anything else. The most common "I paid and got nothing" is a purchase under a different Apple Account or Google account, or under a second account in your own app, and no grant of yours fixes that.

### Why it stuck
- The claim never reached your backend and only a log line knew about it.
- It reached you and threw — an unknown product id after a rename, a purchase made before the user ever signed up — and the exception had nowhere to go.
- The token is already bound to another of their accounts, so your idempotent grant did exactly what it was told.

### Make the ticket your slowest detector
- Dead-letter every failed claim keyed by the store identifier, retry it on a schedule, and alarm on the queue's age. A payment you cannot attribute is parked, never dropped.
- Sweep daily for charges with no entitlement row by walking the store's notification history against your grants.
- Goodwill grants belong in their own table with an operator and a reason. Edit the store-derived row instead and the next `DID_RENEW` silently overwrites the fix.

A charge with no grant is a bug your server can find on its own.

You cannot remote-configure a price — prices live in the stores — so a price test is a server-assigned choice between product ids that already exist, plus a purchase record that remembers which arm produced it.

### Assignment
- Assign on the server, sticky per user (per install while logged out), and return a paywall config: which product ids and offer tokens to fetch, the copy, and the variant id. Bucketing on the client makes the arm unverifiable at readout time.
- The client fetches those ids from the store and renders `displayPrice` or `pricingPhases.formattedPrice`. A price string from your own config is a lie in half the storefronts.
- Ship a default config in the binary. A paywall that cannot render without a network earns nothing on a cold start.
- Every product id in every arm must be live and approved in both stores before the flag flips, and product ids are permanent — you delete an experiment, not the products it created.

### Attribution
- Record the variant on your claim of the purchase, alongside the store identifier. The transaction itself only carries your `appAccountToken` / `obfuscatedAccountId`.
- Revenue events come from server notifications, not the client — the client never sees renewal seven. Attribute every renewal to the arm that produced the original transaction.

### The readout
- Cohort by subscription start, not by calendar week, and report proceeds net of the store's 15–30%, not gross.
- Wait a full billing cycle. Trial starts rise in every arm that widens the trial; conversion, involuntary churn and refunds are what actually decide it.
